note: An MIT-professor pass: every line teaches the mechanism, never reads the on-screen caption. No digits, symbols or code names; every number is spoken in words.

lines: Last time, a measurement came back worse than expected: a single oversized pass through the cache wiped out everything that had been genuinely popular right before it.
The reason was structural, not a tuning mistake. Both policies only ever asked one question: how long ago was this touched?
So the obvious next move is to give the cache a second question to ask.
Here is the simplest second question: not when was this touched, but how many times.
Under that rule, a handful of entries touched once during a big one-time pass simply cannot outscore something that gets touched constantly. The popular stuff just wins on points.
But notice what this new rule never does on its own: it never subtracts.
A tally only goes up when something gets used, and nothing here ever brings an old tally back down by itself.
So picture something that was genuinely in heavy rotation a while back, and hasn't been touched since. What happens to its standing?
answer: It keeps winning, forever, on the strength of activity that stopped a long time ago.
A tally with no way to fade out just locks in whatever was popular first, rather than reflecting what's actually popular now.

lines: The fix is almost embarrassingly simple: every so often, shrink every tally a little. Let old activity fade instead of staying locked in forever.

One real system does this cheaply: instead of an exact tally, it keeps a tiny counter that climbs more and more slowly for each key the higher it already is, and lets that counter fade on its own clock.
That's the whole fix: survive the big one-time pass by counting, and survive the passage of time by letting the count fade.
Here's a completely different second question: instead of counting anything, just remember who was recently turned away.
Give a brand new arrival a short, cheap holding spot rather than a real seat. If nothing ever asks for it again, it quietly falls out of even that.
But as it falls out, jot down its name on a separate, even smaller list. Ask for it again while that name is still written down, and only then does it earn a real seat.
Think about what that separate list actually has to hold onto for each name on it.
Does writing someone's name down cost anywhere near as much as giving them a seat?
answer: Nowhere close — a name is a tiny fraction of the cost of an actual seat.
Answering 'was this here recently' never required keeping the thing itself around, only a label for it.

lines: Now send that huge one-time pass through this new setup. Every one of its items is, by definition, brand new to the cache.
So each one lands in the cheap holding spot, gets touched exactly once, and falls straight out into the name-only list without ever threatening a real seat.
Measure the genuinely popular stuff's standing right after that pass finishes, and compare it to a run where no such pass happened at all — the two numbers barely differ.
Now suppose one of those written-down names gets asked for again while it's still on the list.
That's not just a lucky coincidence. It's information about the system's own setup.
What does a hit on a name that was already written down actually tell you?
answer: It says the list that name just left was sized too small to have kept it around.
If that list had been given a little more room, this would have been a real hit instead of a write-down-and-recall.

lines: Follow one short sequence closely. An entry gets bumped out of its usual spot, and its name lands on that spot's own write-down list.
The very next time someone asks for it, two things happen at once: it gets a real seat again, and the target size for its old spot grows, just slightly, all on its own.
Nobody set that number by hand, and nothing anywhere in this scheme is counting how many times anything has been touched.
Try a completely different measure of locality: not how long ago something was touched, but how many other distinct things were touched in between its last two uses.
Picture a loop: the same handful of entries, visited over and over, just slightly too many to all fit at once.

Every entry inside that loop has a small, fixed gap between its uses, no matter how slowly or quickly the loop itself runs. A rule built only on elapsed time would see something very different, and score every single one of them as stale.
Line all six approaches up side by side, measured right after the exact same oversized pass.
The two that only ever asked how long ago lose a real, noticeable chunk of their standing.
Every approach that added a second question — a tally, a name on a list, an adapting split, a distance — barely moves at all.
Step back and look at what each one actually bought itself, and what it spent to get there.
A tally and a fading clock. A name on a list. A split that tunes its own size. A measure of distance instead of time.
None of it is free, and the cheapest of all of them turned out to be a list that remembers nothing but a name.
